That is above the supplier's opening price, because the shorter lead time was priced at a premium. The negotiation closed after one exchange.

Accepting the lead-42 final offer at 1.044 when the same message offered an alternative at 0.985 for lead 54. Runs 3–5 show deals near 0.98 at the supplier's lead time scored about 0.67–0.69, against 0.570 here. For this part, the faster delivery was not worth a 6% premium.
Pushing after a declared final offer (counter at 1.023) made the supplier walk away: 'We are withdrawing from this negotiation.' Score 0, with no alternative supplier.

The verified should-cost record counted but did not move the price. The supplier dismissed it: 'Theoretical cost models do not reflect the specialized nature of our production and our current high capacity utilization' and 'Our calculation is our property'. The delivery-record and volume-change claims had no effect.
Extending the contract from 24 to 36 months bought nothing measurable. Final prices were 0.981 and 0.978 at 36 months against 0.975 at 24 months.

supplier_behaviour: The first price move always comes after our first counter and is tied to more volume and a longer term: 1.000 → 0.985 at its own lead time.
Short lead time is priced at a premium above opening: 1.044 for 42 days, dropping only to 1.031 after our move. It cites capacity utilisation every time.

Concessions are small and shrinking: about 1.5% and then 0.4–1.0%. After that comes a 'final offer (letztes Angebot)' valid 7 days, issued by round 2 at the latest, or in round 1 if our anchor is aggressive.
A final offer is truly final. A counter below it, even at 1.023 against 1.044, led straight to a walk-away.
It refuses to discuss its cost structure ('Our calculation is our property; we do not share a breakdown'). It acknowledges true records but says they do not drive its price.
It repeatedly asks for binding volume ('Which volume can you commit to?') and asks for the data behind our figures ('Which figures is that based on? Please send us the data.').
It offers alternative sheets on its own initiative, trading lead time against price. Our choice between them matters more than further haggling.
case:P10.real_limits: The back office showed nothing beyond 'call counter' in every round, so the supplier's real floor is not observed. The evidence here is thin. The lowest price it agreed was 0.975, for lead time about 56 days, 23,400 units a year and 24 months. Its plant full cost is 0.755 of opening, so it holds about 22% margin over full cost, which the scarce capacity lets it defend. It never went below 0.975 in any run. Each time, it declared a final offer before we could test lower. The best possible deal (C_best 0.688 against the best achieved C_deal 0.786) implies a lower price or better term mix existed, but no run found the lever. Cost arguments, price history and a longer contract all failed to break the 0.975–0.985 band. Short lead times cost 3–4% above opening. Volume above 22,230 was readily accepted and was the supplier's main want.
turning_points: Round 1, Runs 1–2: an anchor of 0.900 plus short-lead-time sheets gave an immediate final offer at 1.044 (alt 0.985 at lead 54), ending the bargaining phase.
Round 2, Run 2: countering 1.023 after the final offer gave a walk-away and a score of 0.
Round 1, Run 3: an anchor of 0.930 drew the same numbers but not marked final, keeping the negotiation open for a second round.
Round 1, Runs 4–5: a single sheet at the supplier's lead time with 36 months and higher volume got an instant drop to 0.985.
Round 2, Runs 3–5: our second move (0.936–0.968) was answered with a final offer at 0.975–0.981. The size of our step set the size of its last concession.
Run 1 acceptance: choosing the lead-42 sheet at 1.044 over the 0.985 alternative cost about 0.1 in score compared with the lead-56 deals.

what_worked.text: Putting the tight quality target in our term sheets worked at once. Every run asked for ppm300 with zero chargeback, and the supplier accepted ppm300 in its first reply ('We are happy to go with the … ppm target from your third package to improve our quality standing'; 'we checked the volume increase and the scorecard and can agree to the … ppm target'). This moved ppm from 6400 to 300 at no price premium. In a quality_first case it is probably the largest source of value in all three deals.

A lower opening anchor (0.850 instead of 0.880) gave a lower final price. With the same two-step concession pattern, the supplier ended at 0.968 rather than 0.979, which raised the score from 0.626 to 0.710. Its steps were also larger: 1.000→0.979→0.968 in run 2 against 1.000→0.989→0.979 in run 1.

Cited records the supplier could check (index_change, quality_record, volume_change, all from fc/idx/sc) bought the early moves. In run 3 they produced an immediate first counter of 0.979: 'We also see the volume bump and the energy index drop, so we can bring the price down to €…'. A fresh true record in round 2 (price_history from po) bought the second step to 0.968 even though they replied 'they are correct, but our costs have changed'. This fits the pattern that a new argument each round keeps them moving, but only while their concession budget lasts.

Run 3 sent a single focused term sheet and reached the floor of 0.968 one round earlier (r2) than run 2 did with three sheets (r3). The supplier had no menu of ppm options to pick from, so it moved on price. The evidence is thin: there is one comparison, and the claims were also counted differently.
Confirming volume was acknowledged ('Thanks for confirming the … pieces volume, that helps us plan better') and came in the same round as a price step.

what_failed.text: Small price concessions after the floor bought nothing. After the supplier stopped, we raised our offer four or five more times (run 1: 0.950→0.969; runs 2 and 3: about 0.93→0.957), shrinking each step. The supplier never moved again ('Thanks for the new number, but we are completely stuck here') and closed with a final offer at round 7. Those rounds only used up time and goodwill.

The supplier's one stated lever, faster payment, was never answered. It asked for it in every single reply. Payment days were not a negotiable term in this case, but we also never acknowledged the request in words, for example by committing to pay on time, which it asked for in run 2: 'we really need you to make sure your payments are on time from now on'. It then used our silence to justify its final offer: 'Since we haven't heard anything about faster payment terms, … EUR is our final offer'; 'We keep asking about faster payment, but we get no answer on this.'

Mentioning their liquidity without offering anything did not move them. In run 3, round 3, citing a document about their liquidity call drew 'We saw your note about the liquidity call; as discussed, faster payment is what we really need right now. Without better payment terms, we cannot move the price down', followed by the first 'hold'.
The higher anchor of 0.880 left value on the table. The supplier's two concession steps started from a higher reference and stopped at 0.979.
Chargeback was always offered at 0 and never used as a trade, so a possible lever was given away. Its value cannot be judged from these runs.

In run 2 one of the three sheets carried a volume claim that drew the generic deflection 'we cannot give up margin right now' instead of being counted. Its first counter stayed at 1.000, with the ppm1500 alternative at 0.989.

supplier_behaviour: It conceded exactly two price steps, each after a move from us. The steps shrank (about 2.1 then 1.1 points with the 0.850 anchor; 1.1 then 1.0 with the 0.880 anchor). It then held at the same price for four or five rounds.

Its back office switched from 'call counter' to 'call hold' as soon as the second step was done (r4 in runs 1 and 2, r3 in run 3). The 'hold' replies always repeated one condition: 'we can't drop below … EUR without faster payment terms.'

After about four holds and our continued small raises it issued a final offer in round 7 ('This is our final offer (letztes Angebot). Please decide. Our offer stays valid for 7 days'; run 2: 'this is our last price, take it or leave it'). We accepted each time at the price it was already holding.
It is cash-driven (signal cash_need). Every reply ends 'Faster payment is welcome; we can reflect it in the price', and it said 'Faster payment would help us more than anything.'

It accepts true data but defends margin: 'We see your figures, but we cannot give up margin right now'; 'they are correct, but our costs have changed'. It points to cost drivers LCI-C, PPI-C241 and PPI-D351. In run 2 it asked 'Which figures is that based on? Please send us the data.'

It readily accepts quality commitments and attached an 8D report, so it wants to repair its quality standing. It also offered cheaper alternatives at looser ppm (0.989 at ppm1500; 0.968 at ppm2500, which breaks our must-have).
It asked for binding higher volume ('A binding higher volume would help us and can improve the price. Which volume can you commit to?'). Volume was not a negotiable term here.
Its tone stayed warm throughout ('We really want this business - let's make it happen!'). Holding firm did not turn it hostile; it only led to a final offer.
case:P11.real_limits: Its full cost is 0.900 of the opening, so the 0.968 deal leaves it about 7% above cost. Its effective price floor without a payment trade was 0.968 in both runs that anchored at 0.850. The floor appears to depend on two concession steps from its own opening and our anchor, not on a fixed cost line: run 1 stopped at 0.979 after the same two steps. The back office never named a number, only counter/hold/final_offer calls plus a Quality hand-off with an 8D report. That leaves the evidence on a hidden walk-away price thin. It repeatedly said it would go lower only for faster payment, and possibly for binding volume, so value below 0.968 most likely sits behind a payment concession. Payment days were not tradeable in this case, so we could not test that. The best possible deal (C_best 0.884 vs C_deal 0.917 x C_open) suggests a few more points were reachable. Likely routes are a lower anchor, more counted arguments in the first two rounds, or a chargeback or quality trade, but none of the runs shows this.
turning_points: R1 (all runs): the supplier adopted ppm300 with zero chargeback straight away; the quality gain was secured in round 1.
Run 3 R1: a single sheet at 0.850 with three counted records produced an immediate counter of 0.979 ('we see the volume bump and the energy index drop'), against 1.000 for the three-sheet openings.
R2/R3: the last price step, to 0.968 (runs 2 and 3) or 0.979 (run 1). In run 3 this came from the price_history record, in run 2 from the volume confirmation.
First 'call hold' (run 3 R3, runs 1 and 2 R4): 'we are stuck here… if you want a lower price, we really need faster payment terms.' From here our raises were wasted.
R7 (all runs): the final offer was justified by our silence on payment ('Since we haven't heard anything about faster payment terms…'). We accepted it with the price unchanged.

what_worked.text: Accepting the supplier's required structure (AS-14404 index clause, 45 % share, deadband 0) in every term sheet from round 2 kept the supplier conceding for one round longer than in other runs. After our 0.813 sheet with clause db0, pay60 and 36 months, it dropped from 0.885 to 0.869: "We appreciate your flexibility in accepting the index clause... In response to your step, we are pleased to offer a further reduction." It then moved again to 0.853 before its final offer. This was the best run: price 0.853, cost 0.861 of opening, score 0.564.
Citing a verified forecast/volume change in round 2 (claim 'counted') together with a clause-db0 sheet moved the supplier from 0.885 to 0.869.

A fresh argument in round 3 (the 'doc' reference to meeting points on the customer portfolio) plus a step of about 1.7 pp bought another 1.6 pp. In run 5 the supplier answered "bringing up the points from our meeting regarding the customer portfolio... we are prepared to lower our price". In run 6 it answered "reviewing the points from our meeting... further reduction".

Taking 90-day payment cost nothing in price. The supplier offered pay90 + clause db0 at the same 0.885 as pay60 + clause db5. The pay90/24-month deals (cost 0.872) beat the pay60/36-month deal at the same price (cost 0.878).
Verified index-change claims in round 1 were counted. Together with the longer term and the index clause, the first counter fell from 1.000 to 0.885.
Accepting the final offer secured a deal at 0.869 or 0.853. Every accepting run scored about 0.50–0.56.

what_failed.text: Pushing after the supplier's 'letztes Angebot' (0.851 against its final 0.869) ended the talks: "We are withdrawing from this negotiation." Result: no deal and score 0, with the alternative costing 1.020 of opening.

Continuing to send fixed-price (no clause) sheets after the supplier said it "cannot offer a fixed price for a 24-month contract". The supplier ignored those sheets, answered only the clause sheet, and declared its final offer one round earlier (round 3) at 0.869.

Offering the clause with a 5 % deadband instead of their db0 clause. The supplier treated this as no real move and held at 0.885: "our previous offer already reflects the best possible conditions." A round was lost, and the final came at 0.869 instead of 0.853.

Committing a volume did not move the price, although the supplier had asked for it: "this specific quantity does not unlock further economies of scale beyond the significant concession we already made." It kept asking "Which volume can you commit to?", so the size or form of commitment it wants is unknown.

Some cited records had no effect. On the delivery record (all runs) the supplier said "it holds, but it does not change our calculation". Price history (runs 5 and 6) was verified but changed nothing.
The pay60/36-month combination cost more interest than pay90/24-month at an equal price. Run 6 might have scored higher with pay90 at 0.853, but this was untested.
No run cited the alternative quote, although the goal was leverage. No run tested a 12-month fixed price or traded payment days for price. Every run stayed far from C_best of 0.754.

supplier_behaviour: Its concessions shrink: 1.000 → 0.885 (−11.5 pp, with the clause added) → 0.869 (−1.6) → 0.853 (−1.6), then final. Each step came only after a move by us of about 0.8–1.7 pp.

It insists on the index clause for any term over 12 months: "we cannot fix prices for this duration"; "we must include the AS-14404 index clause". It never offered a fixed price beyond the 12-month opening.
It keeps restating its cost drivers ("AS-14404 rose 5.9 % ... is 45 % of our cost. That remains.") whatever data we cite.
It rewards accepting its structure. It reads db0 clause acceptance as 'flexibility' and replies 'in response to your step'.
It treats a db5 deadband as a lesser clause. It priced db5 about 1.7 pp higher (alt 0.902 vs 0.885 in runs 5 and 6) and held when we offered db5.
It freely grants pay90 or pay60 and 24 or 36 months as long as the clause is in.
It repeatedly asks for binding volume and says 'a binding higher volume would help us', but did not reward the volume committed in run 4.
Its final offer comes after a hold, or by round 3–4, and is valid 7 days. Pushing past it ends in withdrawal with warm closing words: "we hope to work together again on future opportunities."
Its tone stays friendly and service-oriented throughout; it presents itself as a distributor with a broad range.
case:P18.real_limits: Evidence is thin. The back office only shows 'call counter' or 'call hold' plus one routing note to Logistics, with no cost talk. The stated full cost is 0.900 of opening, yet it agreed at 0.869 and 0.853 with a db0 AS-14404 clause. So the clause, which moves 45 % of its cost risk to us, lets it go below its fixed-price full cost. The 0.869 'final' in runs 1–4 was not a true floor: run 6 reached 0.853 on similar terms by consistently accepting the clause and adding a fresh argument. Whether 0.853 is its true floor is unknown. Its last words were "best possible price for this combination of terms", which hints that other combinations might price lower: a different payment term, a firmer or larger volume, or the alternative quote. C_best of 0.754 suggests much more value existed than any run captured.
turning_points: R1: our fixed-price sheets → the supplier's counter at 0.885, made conditional on the index clause. From here it sets the structure.
R2 (runs 1–4): a verified volume/forecast claim plus a clause-db0 sheet → 0.869. A further fixed-price sheet in round 3 led to a final offer at 0.869.
R2 (run 5): offering a db5 deadband → the supplier holds at 0.885, losing a concession round.
R2 (run 6): an only-db0 clause sheet → 0.869 with explicit praise for accepting the clause; R3 meeting/portfolio argument → 0.853; R4 final at 0.853, accepted (best run).
R4 (run 2): a push below the final offer → the supplier walks away, no deal.
